newsitem.title: UK: Brief flurry boosts Russia in emerging debt market.
newsitem.headline: Brief flurry boosts Russia in emerging debt market.

text.p: An early flurry of activity briefly pushed up Russian paper on Friday, but it later settled back with the rest of a quiet, though well-underpinned, emerging debt market, traders said.
"Overall the bias (on Russia) is still positive," one U.S. bank trader said.
He said his sales of blocks of Russian paper had met willing buyers this morning.
However, dollar Vneshekonombank debt was back at 78-3/4 cents in the dollar by late morning, unchanged from the New York close.
The positive tone has been on the back of reports of President Boris Yeltsin's recovery from heart surgery at the beginning of the week.
Vnesh has risen more than four points this week, though is still hovering below the 82 cent record it touched last month.

Apart from Yeltsin, the main factors for Russia are its impending Eurobond issue, whether the International Monetary Fund will release more of its loan, and unresolved concerns over the freeze by Russian authorities of stolen MinFin bonds.
"We expect that higher tax revenues since mid-October will convince the upcoming IMF mission that progress had been made," ANZ said it its latest market commentary.
"Russian prices are set to climb over the next few weeks and will go well above the 82 peak set in early October," it added.
There is still no word on when the restructuring of the Vnesh debt will be completed.
"They keep telling me we're on track for closing by the end of this year, but we don't get any specific details," one banker involved in the restructuring negotiations.
Both sides are now in the process of reconciling the about $32 billion of debt.

Under the term sheet, the closing date should be calculated five weeks before the actual closing, which the banker said meant it was very unlikely that the debt would be turned into performing loans this year.
"Noone expects it until February or March," said another banker who follows the issue closely.
Elsewhere, the wait for the outcome of the IMF's current mission in Bulgaria is keeping most investors at bay.
The Bulgarian government is reviewing proposals by the IMF to introduce a currency board.
Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov has said the currency plan was less risky than using high interest rates to prop up the lev.
Traders are mixed between those predicting a jump in the high yielding debt, while others warn that the risk-reward ratio for Bulgarian Bradys is simply not attractive enough for the moment.
The rest of the market is being supported by strong U.S. Treasury bonds.
There was no early impact on Mexican Bradys from the announcement of the country's 1997 budget, which called for greater government spending for the first time since the 1994 peso crisis.
